narratives.Overview:
## Summary

`deft release:run` readiness runs the Phase 2 dry-run **before** the Phase 1 clean working-tree check. On this host the dry-run (or something it invokes) leaves:

- `M .gitignore` (un-ignore rules for `.deft/approved-scope/**`, `.deft/directive/**`, `GENERATION.json`, etc.)
- `?? .deft/GENERATION.json`
- `?? .deft/directive/`

The clean-tree check then refuses even when the tree was clean at entry. Result: readiness always fails after a successful dry-run on a tip cut worktree.

## Observed (v0.131.5 cut)

Fresh worktree at `origin/master` (`30fa5344c`), `git status --porcelain` empty before `release:run`. Dry-run OK (35 fragments folded). Then:

```
[readiness] Phase 1: clean working tree... FAIL (working tree is dirty:)
    M .gitignore
    ?? .deft/GENERATION.json
    ?? .deft/directive/
[readiness] refused: a readiness check failed; nothing was written
```

## Ask

1. Run clean-tree check **before** dry-run, or ignore dry-run-local dirtiness that the cut will not commit.
2. Stop dry-run / readiness from mutating `.gitignore` / writing untracked `.deft/` scratch that fails the same readiness gate.
3. Or accept `--allow-dirty` on `release:run` with an explicit disclosure when the only dirt is that scratch class.

## Workaround used

Manual cut path with `task release -- <version> --allow-dirty` (or clean + re-enter) after operator confirm.

- Operator cut attempt for v0.131.5
- Related: #7326 (github-issue triage cache as hard release preflight)

`deft release:run` readiness is supposed to refuse a dirty tree and write nothing before the cut. On a tip cut worktree the readiness dry-run path still leaves `.gitignore` modified and untracked `.deft/GENERATION.json` / `.deft/directive/`, so the clean-tree gate fails on re-entry (and the cut inherits dirt). 2. Keep the entry clean-tree check; after dry-run returns, re-check clean (or equivalent dirt inventory) and fail readiness with the post-dry-run porcelain when the dry-run path left dirt.

## In plain English

Prefer-A chooses the right repair: keep the initial clean-tree check, stop the dry-run from dirtying the project, and check cleanliness again before proceeding. It needs two changes before binding: cover failed dry-runs and their messages, and require a regression through the actual writer rather than a replacement dry-run function. A post-check alone detects the problem but still leaves the operator blocked.

## Verified mechanisms

Pin-read at `30fa5344c29653f0935703dd28ffdad95e761e27`: `run-readiness.ts/runReleaseReadiness` checks clean before `seams.dryRun`, with no subsequent clean check. `run.ts/defaultReadiness` calls `runPipeline` directly with `dryRun: true` and `allowDirty: false`. In `pipeline.ts`, dry-run skips its own actual clean check, lifecycle scan, CI execution, build and artifact writes; `release-artifacts.ts/prepareReleaseArtifacts` already has a separate read-only dry-run branch. `git.ts/checkGitClean` supplies the reusable porcelain check and fails closed on Git errors. Existing readiness tests stub `dryRun: () => 0` and assert the unconditional no-write message.

These reads verify the ordering and missing post-check, not the reported host-specific writer. I did not execute a release or reproduce the observed files. Inputs were the issue body and comments 7152583302, 7152583577 and 7152605378 only.

## F1 — blocks-the-design: failure exits still violate the promise

Draft item 1 requires neutrality only “when it exits 0.” Yet `formatReadiness` prints “nothing was written” on every failed result, and readiness invokes the dry-run even when an earlier check failed. A dry-run that writes and then returns nonzero can therefore leave P1/P3 intact and repeat P2. Even the proposed post-check's intended dirty result would be followed by that false footer.

Require tree neutrality on successful and failed dry-run exits; run the post-check after any returned dry-run status, preserving both failure details. Remove or qualify the unconditional no-write footer when neutrality is not established. Add the negative regression: a seam introduces dirt and returns nonzero; readiness refuses, reports the dirt and does not claim nothing was written. This is a small extension of the proposed check, not another gate system.

## F2 — blocks-the-design: the regression must exercise the writer

Draft item 4's “runs the readiness dry-run seam” can be satisfied by today's no-op seam. The production pipeline already suppresses several likely writers, so blaming CI/build or merely naming a path would not establish causality. A green stub test plus a post-check could ship while every real tip cut still refuses.

Require the regression to exercise the production dry-run path and the identified writer's triggering condition, stubbing network boundaries as needed, with real filesystem/Git observations. If the writer is in launcher/setup before readiness, include that boundary in the fix and regression. Keep the injected-dirt test separately to prove the guard refuses. Name the actual writer once identified; do not treat the incident report as proof of its call site. Without this, the draft has detection evidence but no demonstrated repair of P1/P3.

## F3 — sharpens-framing: clean porcelain is a narrower guarantee than zero writes

The draft defines neutrality as no tracked changes or newly visible untracked paths. That is a useful release invariant, but `ciReuseAtTip` also performs `git fetch`, and porcelain does not observe ignored-file writes. Absolute “Runs before any write” language overstates what this check proves.

State the guarantee as project working-tree neutrality and keep diagnostic wording within that scope. Under the shared-worktree lens, report dirt observed after dry-run without automatically attributing it to that function, and never erase it with automatic restore/clean: concurrent user changes must survive. This sharpens P2 without requiring a filesystem-wide write monitor.

## Road not taken — footnote

Reorder-only cannot fix the pinned ordering. A narrowly disclosed scratch exception could be justified if the files were proven disposable and outside release inputs, but that proof is absent; `.gitignore` is itself tracked. Broad `--allow-dirty` therefore trades away the relevant protection. Reuse `checkGitClean` plus the existing dry-run branches, fix the actual writer, and retain the post-check.
